To the For Honor Team,

I am writing as a longtime For Honor player with thousands of hours invested in the game. I understand and respect the goal of improving anti-cheat measures and protecting the competitive integrity of Ranked play. I support efforts to stop cheating.

However, I am asking you to reconsider the complete removal of Steam Deck and Linux players from the game.

For Honor is more than just another game to me. Over ten years ago, I met one of my closest friends through For Honor. We spent countless hours fighting side by side, making memories that have stayed with me throughout my life. A few years ago, my friend passed away. Today, For Honor remains one of the strongest connections I have to those memories.

When I purchased a Steam Deck and bought For Honor on Steam, part of my decision was knowing I could continue playing the game that meant so much to both of us. Losing access entirely feels like losing a place that has been important to me for years.

If full Linux support is not possible, I respectfully ask that you consider alternatives:

• Allow Steam Deck and Linux players to access PvE content.
• Allow offline play against bots.
• Allow access to campaign content.
• Allow progression, hero leveling, customization, and collection management.
• Restrict Linux players from Ranked modes if necessary rather than removing access to the entire game.

I am not asking for special treatment. I am only asking for a way to continue experiencing the game and preserving the memories attached to it.

Many Steam Deck and Linux players are not competitors looking for an advantage. We are loyal members of the community who purchased and supported For Honor because we love the game.

Please consider a solution that preserves access for players like me while still achieving your anti-cheat goals.

Thank you for your time and for the years of experiences For Honor has provided.

Sincerely,

A longtime For Honor player

I originally got this game from the free giveaway all the way back in 2018, like many other people. I recently looked at this game again as it popped up in online discourse due to some recent controversies.

On a foundational level, the game is definitely a pretty good game when it comes to meeting its very specific niche. It is a fantasy style action fighting game that people mostly play for the PvP but it does have some campaign elements. It is a game that caters to a very specific audience and that audience definitely seems to like it. Unfortunately for me, it just isn't a game that really clicks and I don't particularly enjoy it all to much. Though, I do have some fond memories of when I originally played it back in 2018. For the average person, it can be an incredibly hard game to get into from a mechanical point of view alongside the relatively low player count that includes a very dedicated existing player base. 

Back to the recent controversies, Ubisoft as a company has definitely never really shied away from them in the last decade or so. There are a variety of ideas that people have issues with For Honor like the microtransaction system, most characters needing to be purchased, in game balancing and optimization issues, required 3rd-party accounts, extensive anti-cheat measures that have an impact on players, and a variety of broader and major company wide issues in real life. The most recent controversy was with the announcement of changes that makes it impossible for the game to run on Linux systems, completely eliminating a portion of the community and the ability for many people who purchased the game to play the game. This includes the ability to play the game on Steam Deck which the game was inadvertently perfect for. 

One smaller issue that really only impacts me is related to the introduction of Steam achievements in 2025. I hadn't played the game since 2018 and wanted to try it out, but as I loaded the game to look at some stuff and idle for cards, I automatically received one achievement that I apparently had met the criteria for back when I originally played. As I have no intention to play the game, nor do I find much joy in playing and have no interest in forcing myself to, my achievements for this game will forever remain at 1%, permanently bringing down my Steam average achievement rate. Ultimately, this isn't something that truly matters but is something that I care about to some extent. Though I suppose, this is just another reality check that I will never be able to get 100% achievements in every game I own as different games have shut down or have achievements that are impossible to get in the modern day. Connected to this, For Honor has achievements requiring DLC that I do not own and have no interest in purchasing.

I do genuinely hope this game stays alive and healthy for those who love it.

I really love this game, I got it as a teenager when it had that free weekend back in the day, but only really got into it a few years ago. There's nothing really like it, its the only fighting game you can play on WiFi reasonably, its fashion is great, some of its maps look amazing (like Canopy and the Belvedere), and despite all the memes, its community is only about as annoying as all the other live service hero "shooters" out there. Its balance team gets chewed out a lot for some of their more controversial characters (Juren, Virtuosa, Varangian Guard, Ocelotl, etc.) and questionable choices (Orange/Blue, Chain on Whiff being the worst offenders), but at the end of the day I do think they actually do a pretty good job, especially with the time, size and money they have.

Unfortunately, I am a Linux player, so on the tenth of September I wont be able to play anymore. The TLDR if you don't know is Windows users gives a lot more information to Ubisoft about your pc and what you're doing (what a linux user would call 'spyware') which allows Ubisoft a better understanding of whose modifying their games and who isnt, but Linux is more protective of personal information. Because of that, even though Linux users are a tiny percentage of the minority pc player base for For Honor, most cheat programs for the game start with a disguise that convinces For Honor that the cheater is on Linux, so they can sneak in easier and be harder to detect. So even though almost all players who cheat are on windows, just like most players who play on pc in general, PC's classified as 'Linux' disproportionately have cheats going on. Their solution is to just not let Linux players play anymore as they launch their Competitive Mode. I'm pretty sure I wont even be able to play offline or against bots, just wont be allowed to boot in general.

I understand *why* they're doing it, since its a small part of the minority player base, but it really is kicking the can down the road. It'll be a minor stopgap in preventing windows cheaters, and cheaters have more time to focus on that, while developers have to focus on making the game, balancing the game, server maintenance, adding new content AND stopping cheaters, on a very small budget and team (despite being one of the only two things seemingly keeping the lights on at Ubisoft alongside Rainbow Six Siege, Source: https://staticctf.ubisoft.com/8aefmxkxpxwl/1LR2VCCkksmsZ3BDdDrpQW/3bbed93696b39f8e2d8cebf527afb025/Ubisoft_FY26_PR_English_vF.pdf) so its one of the simpler, less expensive solutions. The perfect world would have them simply flag pc's marked as Linux, and then pay attention to how often Linux users get reported for cheating specifically. One set of eyes for an hour of footage could probably handle most of this pretty well, but, again, that would be a very expensive solution for a tiny team on a failing company.

As a game, I like it; I don't know if I'd recommend it to most people since it can be pretty frustrating and its got a really niche style, but obviously I can't really recommend this game at all now. I didn't ever buy it or spend money on it, but I do feel worse about the time i put in. They say they might one day bring support back, but they're an overstretched team, i doubt it will be anytime soon unless they cave.

I was aiming to come back to this game at some point to finish up the story and maybe write a proper review, but unfortunately Ubisoft has forced my hand.

I just received an email today that tells me they are ramping up anticheat measures, and so, very soon, 'FOR HONOR' will no longer be available to Linux users.

So for that reason alone: I don't recommend this game.

Now, onto my conspiracy theory.

In this same email, they also shill something called 'Xbox Cloud Gaming'. Here is the full paragraph:

"This means that For Honor will no longer be playable natively on Steam Deck starting September 10. We will keep looking into ways to improve anti-cheating on Linux with the possibility of reopening the platform in the future and in the meantime, we would like to invite you to benefit from cross-progression and join the fight on cloud gaming services like the Xbox Cloud Gaming which runs natively on Steam Deck."

I don't know if you've noticed, but I have noticed a trend personally in the past year or two of random ass games, specifically popular multiplayer games made in the west, games that have not used anticheat or haven't had a reason to use anticheat, etc, so on, suddenly making the decision to go all-in on kernel-level anticheat.

Actually, speaking of which - I wonder if that's what they're planning to implement, since anticheat measures such as EAC and I believe also at least some versions of BattleEye, do actually work on Linux. There's other anticheat solutions as well that work, it's not just those.

Anyway, my conspiracy theory is this, that Microsoft is paying off these publishers, and asking them to implement anticheat into their games, in an effort to help curtail the growing Linux userbase.

The thing that kept most people off of Linux for a very long time, is games. One of the things that built Windows in fact, was games, this is way back in the day. So Microsoft has to be at least partially aware of this thing.

So with the advent of games, like the Battlefield series for example - huge series, very popular - suddenly incorporating kernel-level anticheat plus TPM, Trusted Computing, what have you, I suspect Microsoft is like trying their best to stop a wider Linux adoption by targeting the bigger multiplayer games. Mass appeal video games that, they hope, will kill the Steam Deck and Linux dead.

This is just a conspiracy theory, of course, but it just feels too strange to me that so many games... I mean, look at Battlefield 1, that game is like a decade old now but very recently, in the past year or two, they suddenly added anticheat to it, preventing it from running on Linux computers.

Oh, also I guess this was my 500th review. I guess I'll make a note of that here because that's fun.
